passage:
In the college placement cell, the list showed two offers for Vidya: a logistics firm with a strong training programme, and a small design studio whose recruiter had laughed at her jokes and brought homemade biscuits.
"Studio," Vidya said, before she'd finished reading.
Raghav, from her batch, raised an eyebrow. "Why?"
"Because it's creative. Smaller teams mean more learning. And the location is better."
"The studio's across the city. The firm is next to your hostel."
"Well, commuting builds character." She laughed, then heard herself, reasons tumbling out one after another as if she were hunting for them.
"Did you even read the training part?" Raghav asked.
"No," Vidya admitted. She pulled the sheet back and started from the top.

qa.q: What did the studio's recruiter bring?
qa.a: Homemade biscuits.

qa.q: Why did Vidya choose the studio before finishing the list?
qa.a: The warm recruiter left her with a good feeling, so the studio just felt right, and she hunted for reasons to back it afterward.

qa.q: What could Vidya do before deciding?
qa.a: Read both offers fully, list facts like training and travel for each, and then see whether her gut still agrees.

qa.q: How does Raghav see Vidya's reasons?
qa.a: Raghav notices they don't fit the facts, like the location, and suspects she is defending a choice already made.

grounding: A student picks an internship because the recruiter felt warm, then produces reasons afterwards that do not match the facts.

passage:
Hi Kalyani,

Update: I've found a flatmate! His name's Rudra, and the moment he walked in with a guitar and said the balcony had "good sunset energy", I knew. He just felt right.

You asked if I checked anything. I did, sort of. He's in second-year law, so he must be responsible. He likes the same bands, so we'll get along. And he said he's "pretty clean", which I believe.

Okay, writing that out, I notice every reason arrived after I'd already said yes in my head. Two other people applied with references, and I didn't even call them back.

Maybe I'll call one of them tomorrow. And ask Rudra for a reference. Just to see if the feeling holds up.

Your slightly sheepish brother,
Arnab

qa.q: What did Rudra say about the balcony?
qa.a: That it had "good sunset energy".

qa.q: How does Arnab feel when he realises where his reasons came from?
qa.a: Arnab feels a little sheepish, because he 'just knew' when Rudra walked in, and the reasons like the law course and shared bands only arrived after the yes.

qa.q: What checks does Arnab plan, and what else could help?
qa.a: Calling one of the applicants with references and asking Rudra for one; agreeing on house rules before signing could also help.

qa.q: Why might Kalyani have asked if Arnab checked anything?
qa.a: She probably knows her brother goes with his gut and worries that a friendly first impression isn't enough for sharing a home.

grounding: A student chooses a flatmate because he felt right, then notices in an email that all the reasons were built afterwards.

passage:
Kavitha, you'll laugh. Remember I said I'd compare five second-hand scooters? I saw the first one, mint green, and the seller's grandmother gave me tea, and that was it. I paid the advance that evening.
Then I spent the whole bus ride home convincing myself. Green is easy to spot in traffic, so it's safer. Older scooters are sturdier. That grandmother would never sell a bad one. I'd built a whole case, like a lawyer for my own feelings.
Then my brother asked, "Shalini, did you check the brakes?" I hadn't. I hadn't even checked the papers.
So tomorrow I'm going back with the mechanic from our lane. If it passes, great. If not, I lose the advance, and I'll live.

qa.q: What colour was the scooter Shalini chose?
qa.a: Mint green.

qa.q: What does 'a lawyer for my own feelings' reveal about Shalini's thinking?
qa.a: Shalini sees that the choice came from a warm feeling about the colour and the tea, and the reasons were gathered afterwards to defend it.

qa.q: Is going back with the mechanic a good plan? Why?
qa.a: Yes; it lets facts like the brakes and papers test the gut choice before Shalini rides it, even if the advance is lost.

qa.q: How might Shalini's brother see the purchase?
qa.a: He likely sees an exciting buy made without basic checks, and cares more about the brakes than the colour.

grounding: Shalini buys a scooter on a warm feeling, builds reasons afterwards, then plans a proper check.

passage: I'm Lalit, Santosh's roommate in the Bengaluru hostel, and I watched this happen last month. Santosh had two offers for a part-time job: a café in Koramangala and the college library. The library paid more and was two minutes away. But Santosh walked into the café once, saw the warm lights and the plants, and the manager joked with him. He came back glowing. "That's the one. It just feels right." The next day he had a whole list: "Customer skills, networking, great for my CV." I asked, "Did you think of those before or after?" He laughed and threw a pillow at me. I don't know what was going on in his head. But those reasons definitely weren't there the first evening, and nobody mentioned the forty-minute bus ride.

qa.q: What did Santosh see when he walked into the café?
qa.a: The warm lights and the plants, and the manager joked with him.

qa.q: Why did the café "just feel right" to Santosh?
qa.a: The warm, friendly place gave him a good feeling, and that feeling made the choice seem obvious before he thought about pay or distance.

qa.q: What question could Santosh ask before his next big choice?
qa.a: He could write down the facts, like pay and travel time, before visiting, and then ask whether his reasons came before or after the feeling.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the list Santosh made the next day?
qa.a: Lalit suspects the reasons were built afterwards to support a choice already made by feeling, especially since the bus ride was never mentioned.

grounding: A roommate watches a student pick a job because it feels right and then come up with reasons afterward.

subtype: Gut feeling on people and products [Actor]
passage:
Saturday: At the phone market in Lucknow, Harish, twenty, picked up a slim black phone and felt a small thrill. "This one," he told Ojas. The shopkeeper hadn't even switched it on.
Monday: Harish made a comparison sheet on his laptop. The black phone won on "looks premium," "good for interviews," "feels solid." The grey one's better battery he wrote down as "not a big deal." He showed Ojas proudly. Ojas raised an eyebrow. "You decided on Saturday. This is just a costume for it."
Two weeks later: At 3 p.m., in the middle of a lab, the black phone died. Harish sat on the corridor steps, charger-less, and texted from Ojas's phone: "Okay. Maybe I picked it and then found reasons." Ojas sent back a thumbs up and a battery emoji.

qa.q: When did the black phone die?
qa.a: At 3 p.m., in the middle of a lab, two weeks later.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about the black phone, and how did that change?
qa.a: Harish felt a small thrill and was proud of the sheet that backed his choice, but when the phone died mid-lab he felt stuck and admitted he picked it first and found reasons later.

qa.q: What could Harish do differently before buying something next time?
qa.a: He could list what really matters, like battery life, before he goes to the shop, so the good feeling doesn't choose first.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel reading Harish's text from the corridor?
qa.a: Ojas is probably amused and a little satisfied at being proved right, but still friendly, sending a thumbs up.

grounding: Over two weeks a student picks a phone because it feels right, builds reasons afterward, and later admits it.
